passage: Gargi had moved to Mumbai in January, and in the third week of March everything went wrong at once. On Monday her pitch was rejected in front of the whole client team. On Tuesday the fever started. By Wednesday night she lay in her rented room in Andheri, sheets damp, kettle empty, rain hammering on the tin sunshade. No Maa bringing rasam, no cousin two streets away. She scrolled flights home and whispered, 'What was I thinking, coming here?' Her thumb hovered over Neelam's name, the quiet designer from the next desk; they had shared lunch exactly twice. She typed, 'Sorry, bit random, I'm unwell and alone, is there a chemist that delivers?' Neelam called within minutes and arrived an hour later with soup, a thermometer and the number of a nearby clinic. 'If it doesn't settle, we'll go together,' Neelam said. Gargi cried from relief.

qa.a: Soup, a thermometer and the number of a nearby clinic.

qa.q: What does Gargi scrolling flights home suggest about her state of mind?
qa.a: Her doubt about the move had peaked; ill and alone after a setback, she questioned why she had come at all.

qa.q: What turned the stretch for Gargi?
qa.a: Reaching out to Neelam, though they barely knew each other, brought care and a plan to see a doctor together if the fever did not settle.

qa.q: What might it be like for Neelam to get Gargi's message?
qa.a: Neelam may be surprised but moved to be trusted, and responds quickly, perhaps knowing how alone a new city can feel.

grounding: Shows a low point after a work setback and illness in a new city, where doubt peaks and reaching out to a colleague turns things.

passage:
'Chandu akka, don't panic, okay?' Sachin said, his face grey on the video call.
'Now I'm panicking. What happened?'
'The project I've been on since I moved here got scrapped. Four months, gone. And the landlord says the flat's being sold.'
'Oh, Sachin.'
'I don't know anyone here to even rant to. I walked around Hitech City for two hours so I wasn't just sitting in the room.'
'Have you eaten?'
'Chips.'
'Sachin.'
He laughed weakly. 'I keep thinking I should just come back to Vizag. Maybe this was a mistake.'
'Maybe. Maybe not. Don't decide in your worst week.' Chandrika pulled her laptop closer. 'Tonight, order real food. Tomorrow, call that college senior you mentioned, Ravi. And call me every evening this week, even for two minutes.'
'Every evening?'
'Every evening. I'm your net until you build one here.'

qa.q: How long did Sachin walk around Hitech City?
What is Sachin worried he got wrong at this point?
qa.a: He doubts the move itself, wondering if coming was a mistake after losing his project and his flat in the same week.

qa.q: What does Chandrika's advice get right?
qa.a: She tells him not to decide in his worst week and gives small steps: real food, a call to Ravi and a daily check-in with her.

qa.q: What is it like for Chandrika to see her brother this low?
qa.a: She is worried and briefly panicked, yet steadies herself to be his support until he builds his own 🫂

grounding: Illustrates the low point of a move, when a work setback and housing trouble without local support make doubt peak, and reaching out helps.
